slides.title: Your *amount field* won't activate?
slides.voiceover: Stop: your amount field fails activation in SE11. Last time we learned the primary key. Now, currency and quantity fields.
slides.spoken: Stop: your amount field fails activation in SE11. Last time we learned the primary key. Now, currency and quantity fields.

slides.label: WHY
slides.heading: 100 *what?*
slides.body: An amount without a currency means nothing: 100 EUR or 100 JPY?
slides.voiceover: Why? An amount of one hundred means nothing. Euros? Yen? SAP needs the currency right next to it.
slides.spoken: Why? An amount of 100 means nothing. Euros? Yen? SAP needs the currency right next to it.

slides.label: NEW TERM
slides.heading: Every amount needs a *partner*
slides.voiceover: A CURR field alone fails the activation check. SE11 refuses it. It needs a reference field: a CUKY field that holds the currency.
slides.spoken: A CURR field alone fails the activation check. SE11 refuses it. It needs a reference field: a CUKY field that holds the currency.

slides.heading: The *Currency/Quantity* tab
slides.voiceover: Click the Currency/Quantity Fields tab. For NETWR, enter reference table VBAK and reference field WAERK.
slides.spoken: Click the Currency/Quantity Fields tab. For NETWR, enter reference table VBAK and reference field WAERK.

slides.title: Currency/Quantity Fields
slides.voiceover: Real example: in VBAK, the net value NETWR points to WAERK. In VBAP, the quantity KWMENG points to the unit VRKME.
slides.spoken: Real example: in VBAK, the net value NETWR points to WAERK. In VBAP, the quantity KWMENG points to the unit VRKME.

slides.label: COMMON MISTAKE
slides.heading: A *CHAR* field as partner
slides.voiceover: Common mistake: pointing to a plain CHAR field. The partner must be CUKY for amounts and UNIT for quantities.
slides.spoken: Common mistake: pointing to a plain CHAR field. The partner must be CUKY for amounts and UNIT for quantities.

slides.label: REMEMBER
slides.heading: Amounts come in *pairs*
slides.voiceover: Takeaway: every amount needs a currency, and every quantity needs a unit.
slides.spoken: Takeaway: every amount needs a currency, and every quantity needs a unit.

SAP ABAP tables, Part 9 of 18: currency and quantity fields in SE11.

1. A CURR field needs a reference field of type CUKY (the currency)
2. A QUAN field needs a reference field of type UNIT (the unit)
3. Set both on the Currency/Quantity Fields tab: reference table + reference field
4. Example: VBAK-NETWR points to WAERK, VBAP-KWMENG to VRKME
5. Common mistake: a plain CHAR field as the partner

slides.title: BAPI said *saved* but VA03 says no
slides.voiceover: The BAPI said saved. Order one-two-three-four-five doesn't exist.
slides.spoken: The BAPI said saved. Order 12345 doesn't exist.

slides.err: SD document 12345 is not in the database or has been archived
slides.voiceover: RETURN says standard order saved. The program ends. You open VA03, and the order isn't there.
slides.spoken: RETURN says Standard Order 12345 has been saved. The program ends. You open VA03, and the order isn't there.

slides.label: WHY
slides.heading: BAPIs *don't commit*
slides.body: Most BAPIs only queue the change. No COMMIT = it's thrown away when the program ends.
slides.voiceover: Why? Most BAPIs don't commit. They only queue the change. No commit, and it's thrown away at the end.
slides.spoken: Why? Most BAPIs don't commit. They only queue the change. No commit, and it's thrown away at the end.

slides.heading: Check, then *commit*
slides.code:
IF NOT line_exists( lt_ret[ type = 'E' ] ).
  CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT'
    EXPORTING wait = abap_true.
ELSE.
  CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK'.
ENDIF.
slides.voiceover: The fix: check RETURN for errors. No errors? Call BAPI transaction commit, with wait. Errors? Roll back.
slides.spoken: The fix: check RETURN for errors. No errors? Call BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT, with wait. Errors? Roll back.

slides.label: COMMON MISTAKE
slides.heading: Commit *without wait*

bad.title: COMMIT, no WAIT
bad.sub: the next read may not find the order yet

good.title: wait = abap_true
good.sub: the update finishes before you go on

slides.voiceover: Common mistake: committing without wait. Your next read may not find the order yet. Set wait, and the update finishes first.
slides.spoken: Common mistake: committing without wait. Your next read may not find the order yet. Set wait, and the update finishes first.

slides.label: TAKEAWAY
slides.heading: The BAPI *ritual*
slides.voiceover: Takeaway: call, check RETURN, commit. For every BAPI that changes data.
slides.spoken: Takeaway: call, check RETURN, commit. For every BAPI that changes data.

posts.caption:
The BAPI said saved. Order 12345 doesn't exist.

A classic SAP ABAP BAPI bug: no BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT.

1. Most BAPIs only queue the change, they don't commit
2. Check RETURN for type E messages
3. No errors: BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT with WAIT = abap_true
4. Errors: BAPI_TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK
5. Without WAIT, the next read may not see the document yet

Save this for your next BAPI call.

slides.title: Two answers *before* activation
slides.voiceover: Your table needs two answers before it activates. Last time we learned currency and quantity fields. Now, technical settings.
slides.spoken: Your table needs two answers before it activates. Last time we learned currency and quantity fields. Now, technical settings.

slides.heading: Open *Technical Settings*
slides.voiceover: Why? The database must know what you store and how much. In SE11, click Technical Settings. Two fields: data class and size category.
slides.spoken: Why? The database must know what you store and how much. In SE11, click Technical Settings. Two fields: data class and size category.

slides.label: NEW TERM
slides.heading: *Data class*
slides.body: Data class = what kind of data the table holds, so the database keeps it in the right area.
slides.voiceover: A data class tells the database what kind of data your table holds.
slides.spoken: A data class tells the database what kind of data your table holds.

slides.label: EXAMPLE
slides.heading: Every table on its *shelf*
slides.voiceover: APPL0 is master data, like MARA. APPL1 is transaction data, like VBAK. APPL2 is customizing, like T001.
slides.spoken: APPL0 is master data, like MARA. APPL1 is transaction data, like VBAK. APPL2 is customizing, like T001.

slides.label: NEW TERM
slides.heading: *Size category* 0 to 9
slides.voiceover: Size category is how many rows you expect, from zero to nine. Press F4 to see the row range for each one.
slides.spoken: Size category is how many rows you expect, from 0 to 9. Press F4 to see the row range for each one.

slides.label: COMMON MISTAKE
slides.heading: Size *0* for a log table

bad.title: Size category 0
bad.sub: for a table that grows to millions

good.title: Pick by expected rows
good.sub: F4 shows the range per category

slides.voiceover: Common mistake: size category zero for a table that grows to millions of rows. Pick it by the rows you expect.
slides.spoken: Common mistake: size category zero for a table that grows to millions of rows. Pick it by the rows you expect.

slides.label: REMEMBER
slides.heading: *What* and *how much*
slides.voiceover: Takeaway: data class says what kind of data. Size category says how much.
slides.spoken: Takeaway: data class says what kind of data. Size category says how much.

slides.title: Read T001 *without the database*
slides.voiceover: Stop reading T001 from the database ten times. Last time we learned technical settings. Now, buffering.
slides.spoken: Stop reading T001 from the database ten times. Last time we learned technical settings. Now, buffering.

slides.label: NEW TERM
slides.heading: The *table buffer*
slides.body: Table buffer = a copy of table rows in the application server's memory.
slides.voiceover: Why? Every database read takes time. The table buffer is a copy of the rows in the application server's memory.
slides.spoken: Why? Every database read takes time. The table buffer is a copy of the rows in the application server's memory.

slides.label: EXAMPLE
slides.heading: First read vs *next read*
slides.voiceover: First read: the SELECT goes to the database and fills the buffer. Next read: straight from memory. Much faster.
slides.spoken: First read: the SELECT goes to the database and fills the buffer. Next read: straight from memory. Much faster.

slides.label: TECHNICAL SETTINGS
slides.heading: Three *switches*
slides.title: Buffering
slides.voiceover: In technical settings, pick one. Not allowed: never buffered. Allowed but switched off: possible, but off. Switched on: buffered.
slides.spoken: In technical settings, pick one. Not allowed: never buffered. Allowed but switched off: possible, but off. Switched on: buffered.

slides.label: BUFFERING TYPE
slides.heading: How *much* is buffered
slides.voiceover: Then pick the type. Single records: only the rows you read. Generic area: rows sharing the first key fields. Fully buffered: the whole table.
slides.spoken: Then pick the type. Single records: only the rows you read. Generic area: rows sharing the first key fields. Fully buffered: the whole table.

slides.label: COMMON MISTAKE
slides.heading: Buffering *VBAK*

bad.title: Buffer VBAK
bad.sub: changes all day, other servers read old rows

slides.voiceover: Common mistake: buffering a table that changes all day, like VBAK. Other servers can read old rows. Buffer small tables you mostly read, like T001.
slides.spoken: Common mistake: buffering a table that changes all day, like VBAK. Other servers can read old rows. Buffer small tables you mostly read, like T001.

slides.label: REMEMBER
slides.heading: Read often, *change rarely*
slides.body: Buffer small tables that are read often and changed rarely. Never buffer transaction data.
slides.voiceover: Takeaway: buffer what's read often and changed rarely.
slides.spoken: Takeaway: buffer what's read often and changed rarely.
